CHARACTERIZATION AND DIVISION OF A PERSONAL INJURY RECOVERY IN MARRIAGE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Personal Injury Recovery Characterization Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, whose marital dissolution or legal separation proceeding is pending, or may be filed, in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It describes what the California Family Code and published California appellate decisions say about how money or other property received in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for personal injuries — or under an agreement settling or compromising a claim for those damages — is characterized as community or separate property, and how such a recovery is assigned when the community estate is divided. This information sheet states what the law says in general terms. It does not determine, calculate, or assert when any cause of action of Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee arose, how any particular recovery should be characterized, whether any recovery has been commingled with other assets of the community estate, or how any recovery should be assigned; those are matters for the court to decide on the specific facts, or for Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee to resolve by their own written agreement.

THE GENERAL RULE: A RECOVERY ON A CAUSE OF ACTION THAT AROSE DURING THE MARRIAGE IS COMMUNITY PROPERTY
Family Code section 780 states the general characterization rule for personal injury recoveries between spouses. Money and other property received, or to be received, by a married person in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for personal injuries, or under an agreement settling or compromising a claim for those damages, is community property if the cause of action for the damages arose during the marriage. The section states two express qualifications on its own face: it applies "[e]xcept as provided in Section 781," the section that makes certain recoveries the injured person’s separate property, and it is "subject to the rules of allocation set forth in Section 2603," the section that governs how such a recovery is assigned when the community estate is divided. Both of those sections are described in this document’s later clauses. Under the text of section 780, the timing of the cause of action — not the timing of the payment — is what the characterization rule turns on, because the section reaches money "received or to be received."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Except as provided in Section 781 and subject to the rules of allocation set forth in Section 2603, money and other property received or to be received by a married person in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for personal injuries, or pursuant to an agreement for the settlement or compromise of a claim for such damages, is community property if the cause of action for the damages arose during the marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 780 (California Legislative Information text), the general rule characterizing a personal injury recovery as community property when the cause of action arose during the marriage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=780.)

The section states the rule but does not itself define when a cause of action "arose," does not define "personal injuries," and does not address recoveries that are not damages for personal injuries (for example, purely economic-loss recoveries, workers’ compensation benefits, or disability benefits); this document addresses the "arose" timing question, and the boundary against workers’ compensation permanent disability awards, only to the extent the California appellate decisions cited in this document’s later clauses addressed them. The citations in this clause and in the clauses quoting sections 781, 782, 783, and 2603 are all to sections of one code enacted by one statute (Stats. 1992, ch. 162), and are not independent of one another.

WHEN THE RECOVERY IS THE INJURED PERSON’S SEPARATE PROPERTY INSTEAD
Family Code section 781, subdivision (a), states the exception to the general rule. A recovery for personal injuries — whether received in satisfaction of a judgment or under an agreement settling or compromising the claim — is the separate property of the injured person if the cause of action for the damages arose either after the entry of a judgment of dissolution of a marriage or legal separation of the parties, or while the injured spouse is living separate from the other spouse. The statutory line is drawn by when the cause of action arose, so a cause of action that arose while the injured spouse was living separate from the other spouse falls within the subdivision even though no judgment had yet been entered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Money or other property received or to be received by a married person in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for personal injuries, or pursuant to an agreement for the settlement or compromise of a claim for those damages, is the separate property of the injured person if the cause of action for the damages arose as follows: (1) After the entry of a judgment of dissolution of a marriage or legal separation of the parties. (2) While the injured spouse is living separate from the other spouse."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 781(a) (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (a), the two circumstances in which a personal injury recovery is the injured person’s separate property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=781.)

REIMBURSEMENT FOR EXPENSES PAID, AND RECOVERIES BETWEEN THE SPOUSES THEMSELVES
Family Code section 781 attaches two further rules to the separate-property characterization in subdivision (a). First, subdivision (b) provides that if the spouse of the injured person has paid expenses by reason of the personal injuries — whether from separate property or from the community property — that spouse is entitled to reimbursement of the separate property or the community property for those expenses, payable from the separate property the injured person received under subdivision (a). Second, subdivision (c) addresses claims between the spouses themselves: where one spouse has a cause of action against the other spouse that arose during the marriage, money or property paid by or on behalf of a party to that party’s spouse in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for personal injuries to that spouse, or under an agreement settling or compromising the claim, is the separate property of the injured spouse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), if the spouse of the injured person has paid expenses by reason of the personal injuries from separate property or from the community property, the spouse is entitled to reimbursement of the separate property or the community property for those expenses from the separate property received by the injured person under subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 781(b) (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (b), reimbursement of separate or community property for expenses paid by reason of the personal injuries (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=781.)
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), if one spouse has a cause of action against the other spouse that arose during the marriage of the parties, money or property paid or to be paid by or on behalf of a party to the party’s spouse of that marriage in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for personal injuries to that spouse, or pursuant to an agreement for the settlement or compromise of a claim for the damages, is the separate property of the injured spouse."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 781(c) (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (c), a recovery on one spouse’s cause of action against the other spouse arising during the marriage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=781.)

WHAT "COMMUNITY ESTATE PERSONAL INJURY DAMAGES" MEANS — AND THE COMMINGLING LIMIT
Family Code section 2603, subdivision (a), supplies the definition used by the assignment rule that follows it. "Community estate personal injury damages," as used in that section, means all money or other property received or to be received by a person in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for the person’s personal injuries, or under an agreement settling or compromising a claim for the damages, if the cause of action for the damages arose during the marriage but is not separate property as described in section 781. The definition carries an express exception on its own face: it does not reach money or other property that "has been commingled with other assets of the community estate." By the statute’s own terms, then, a recovery that satisfies the definition is treated under the special assignment rule described in the next clause, while a recovery that has been commingled with other community assets falls outside the definition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "“Community estate personal injury damages” as used in this section means all money or other property received or to be received by a person in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for the person’s personal injuries or pursuant to an agreement for the settlement or compromise of a claim for the damages, if the cause of action for the damages arose during the marriage but is not separate property as described in Section 781, unless the money or other property has been commingled with other assets of the community estate."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2603(a) (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (a), the statutory definition of "community estate personal injury damages" and its commingling exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2603.)

THE ASSIGNMENT RULE: TO THE INJURED PARTY UNLESS THE INTERESTS OF JUSTICE REQUIRE OTHERWISE
Family Code section 2603, subdivision (b), states how community estate personal injury damages are assigned. The default is that they shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries. The court may order another disposition only if, after taking into account three things the statute names — the economic condition and needs of each party; the time that has elapsed since the recovery of the damages or the accrual of the cause of action; and all other facts of the case — it determines that the interests of justice require another disposition. If the court makes that determination, the damages are assigned to the respective parties in such proportions as the court determines to be just, subject to a floor stated in the statute itself: at least one-half of the damages shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Community estate personal injury damages shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries unless the court, after taking into account the economic condition and needs of each party, the time that has elapsed since the recovery of the damages or the accrual of the cause of action, and all other facts of the case, determines that the interests of justice require another disposition. In such a case, the community estate personal injury damages shall be assigned to the respective parties in such proportions as the court determines to be just, except that at least one-half of the damages shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2603(b) (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (b), the assignment rule, the enumerated factors, and the one-half floor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2603.)

A COURT OF APPEAL HELD THE ASSIGNMENT RULE IS AN EXCEPTION TO EQUAL DIVISION, NOT AN OFFSET
In In re Marriage of Morris (1983) 139 Cal.App.3d 823, the Court of Appeal considered a dissolution in which the trial court divided the other community property equally and awarded the entire $42,987.72 received in settlement of the wife’s personal injury claims to her. The husband argued that the assignment provision was meant only to ensure the injured spouse received a liquid asset, so that he should have received offsetting community property to equalize the division. The Court of Appeal rejected that reading and affirmed, holding that the provision directing that community property personal injury damages "shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries" was intended to be an exception to the equal division mandate. The court also described what the provision is designed to do: assure that, other than in exceptional circumstances, such damages or the bulk of them will be awarded to the injured spouse, and that under no circumstances will the injured spouse receive less than one-half, while leaving the court discretion in exceptional circumstances to assign the damages in such proportions as it determines to be just.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "we agree with the Mason court, Judge Markey and the trial court in this case that the statutory provision that community property personal injury damages “shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries” was intended to be an exception to the equal division mandate found in subdivision (a) of section 4800."
  — In re Marriage of Morris (1983) 139 Cal.App.3d 823, 139 Cal.App.3d 823, 828 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2178661/in-re-marriage-of-morris/)
  "The statute is designed to assure that other than in exceptional circumstances, community property personal injury damages, or the bulk thereof, will be awarded to the injured spouse and that under no circumstances will the injured spouse receive less than one-half of such damages."
  — In re Marriage of Morris (1983) 139 Cal.App.3d 823, 139 Cal.App.3d 823, 827 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2178661/in-re-marriage-of-morris/)

A COURT OF APPEAL DISTINGUISHED WHEN A CAUSE OF ACTION "AROSE" FROM WHEN IT "ACCRUED"
Both the community-property rule of section 780 and the separate-property rule of section 781 turn on when the cause of action "arose." In Klug v. Klug (2005) 130 Cal.App.4th 1389, the Court of Appeal addressed a postjudgment motion to divide an allegedly omitted community asset — a $346,000 settlement of one spouse’s legal malpractice lawsuit against the couple’s former attorney — and set out the framework of sections 780, 781, and 2603. The court stated that for purposes of a motion to divide an omitted asset, the characterization of tort damages as separate or community property turns on when the cause of action arose. It then distinguished "arose" from "accrued," explaining that a cause of action may arise when the wrongful conduct causes damage even though, under the delayed-discovery rules that govern statutes of limitation, the same cause of action does not accrue until the injured person discovers or should discover the facts. The court concluded that it could think of no policy reason why characterization of a property interest as community or separate should depend on the date of discovery rather than the date all the elements of the cause of action were established, and it affirmed the order treating the settlement as the injured spouse’s separate property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "For purposes of applying section 2556, the characterization of tort damages as separate or community property turns on when the cause of action arose."
  — Klug v. Klug (In re Marriage of Klug) (2005) 130 Cal.App.4th 1389, 130 Cal.App.4th 1389, 1396 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5809278/klug-v-klug/)
  "We can think of no policy reason why the characterization of a property interest as community or separate should depend on the date of discovery of the injury rather than the date all the elements of the cause of action were established."
  — Klug v. Klug (In re Marriage of Klug) (2005) 130 Cal.App.4th 1389, 130 Cal.App.4th 1389, 1400 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5809278/klug-v-klug/)

This document does not assert that every kind of tort claim is governed by sections 780 and 781, and does not address the elements or accrual rules of legal malpractice claims, which are outside its scope. A COURT OF APPEAL TREATED UNINSURED MOTORIST PROCEEDS AS COMMUNITY ESTATE PERSONAL INJURY DAMAGES
In In re Marriage of Jackson (1989) 212 Cal.App.3d 479, the parties were injured in a collision with an uninsured driver, and the injured spouse received proceeds under the uninsured motorist coverage of a policy the community had paid for. The uninjured spouse argued that those proceeds were ordinary community property subject to equal division, because the statutory definition of "community estate personal injury damages" speaks of a judgment or a settlement of a claim for damages and does not mention uninsured motorist coverage. The Court of Appeal disagreed, reasoning that an agreement with the injured party’s own insurer was the equivalent of a settlement with the tortfeasor, and concluded that the sums received in settlement of the uninsured motorist claim were community estate personal injury damages, so that the trial court was free to divide them under the special assignment statute. The court added that the community’s payment of the policy premiums did not compel a different result.

A BOUNDARY: A COURT OF APPEAL HELD A WORKERS’ COMPENSATION DISABILITY AWARD IS NOT A PERSONAL INJURY RECOVERY UNDER THESE SECTIONS
Not every payment that follows an injury is governed by the personal injury characterization statutes. In In re Marriage of Fisk (1992) 2 Cal.App.4th 1698, a spouse sought a share of, or reimbursement from, a workers’ compensation permanent disability award the other spouse received after the parties separated. The Court of Appeal held that such an award received after separation compensates the injured person for impairment of future earning capacity and is that person’s separate property, and that the reimbursement provision then codified at former Civil Code section 5126, subdivision (b), did not apply. The court reasoned that a workers’ compensation permanent disability award is distinguishable from a personal injury recovery at law — among other reasons, because it is awarded without regard to fault — and that such a disability award therefore cannot be embraced within the term "damages" used in the section’s reimbursement requirement. In a footnote, the court added that the predecessor of section 2603 likewise applies only to personal injury awards in actions at law and had no application to the award.

WHICH PROPERTY ANSWERS FOR THE LIABILITY WHEN ONE SPOUSE INJURES THE OTHER
Family Code section 782 addresses the source of funds that answers for a liability when an injury to a married person is caused in whole or in part by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of that person’s spouse. Subdivision (a) provides that the community property may not be used to discharge the tortfeasor spouse’s liability to the injured spouse, or the liability to make contribution to a joint tortfeasor, until the separate property of the tortfeasor spouse that is not exempt from enforcement of a money judgment is exhausted. Subdivision (b) states an exception: the section does not prevent the use of community property to discharge such a liability if the injured spouse gives written consent after the occurrence of the injury. Subdivision (c) provides that the section does not affect the right to indemnity provided by an insurance or other contract to discharge the tortfeasor spouse’s liability, whether or not the consideration given for the contract consisted of community property.

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 782(a) (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (a), exhaustion of the tortfeasor spouse’s separate property before community property is used (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=782.)

A SPOUSE’S CONCURRING NEGLIGENCE IS NOT A DEFENSE FOR A THIRD PARTY BECAUSE OF THE MARRIAGE
Family Code section 783 addresses an action by an injured married person against a third party. Where a married person is injured by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of someone other than that person’s spouse, the fact that the spouse’s negligent or wrongful act or omission was a concurring cause of the injury is not a defense in the injured person’s action against the third party. The section states one express qualification: the concurring negligence remains a defense in cases where it would be a defense if the marriage did not exist.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "If a married person is injured by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of a person other than the married person’s spouse, the fact that the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the spouse of the injured person was a concurring cause of the injury is not a defense in an action brought by the injured person to recover damages for the injury except in cases where the concurring negligent or wrongful act or omission would be a defense if the marriage did not exist."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 783 (California Legislative Information text), the rule that a spouse’s concurring negligence is not a defense to the injured person’s action against a third party (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=783.)

It describes what the California Family Code and published California appellate decisions say about how money or other property received in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for personal injuries — or under an agreement settling or compromising a claim for those damages — is characterized as community or separate property, and how such a recovery is assigned when the community estate is divided. This information sheet states what the law says in general terms. It does not determine, calculate, or assert when any cause of action of Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee arose, how any particular recovery should be characterized, whether any recovery has been commingled with other assets of the community estate, or how any recovery should be assigned; those are matters for the court to decide on the specific facts, or for Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee to resolve by their own written agreement.

Family Code section 780 states the general characterization rule for personal injury recoveries between spouses. Money and other property received, or to be received, by a married person in satisfaction of a judgment for damages for personal injuries, or under an agreement settling or compromising a claim for those damages, is community property if the cause of action for the damages arose during the marriage. The section states two express qualifications on its own face: it applies "[e]xcept as provided in Section 781," the section that makes certain recoveries the injured person’s separate property, and it is "subject to the rules of allocation set forth in Section 2603," the section that governs how such a recovery is assigned when the community estate is divided. Both of those sections are described in this document’s later clauses. Under the text of section 780, the timing of the cause of action — not the timing of the payment — is what the characterization rule turns on, because the section reaches money "received or to be received."

A recovery for personal injuries — whether received in satisfaction of a judgment or under an agreement settling or compromising the claim — is the separate property of the injured person if the cause of action for the damages arose either after the entry of a judgment of dissolution of a marriage or legal separation of the parties, or while the injured spouse is living separate from the other spouse. The statutory line is drawn by when the cause of action arose, so a cause of action that arose while the injured spouse was living separate from the other spouse falls within the subdivision even though no judgment had yet been entered.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 2603, subdivision (b), states how community estate personal injury damages are assigned. The default is that they shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries. The court may order another disposition only if, after taking into account three things the statute names — the economic condition and needs of each party; the time that has elapsed since the recovery of the damages or the accrual of the cause of action; and all other facts of the case — it determines that the interests of justice require another disposition. If the court makes that determination, the damages are assigned to the respective parties in such proportions as the court determines to be just, subject to a floor stated in the statute itself: at least one-half of the damages shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries.

In such a case, the community estate personal injury damages shall be assigned to the respective parties in such proportions as the court determines to be just, except that at least one-half of the damages shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Morris (1983) 139 Cal.App.3d 823, the Court of Appeal considered a dissolution in which the trial court divided the other community property equally and awarded the entire $42,987.72 received in settlement of the wife’s personal injury claims to her. The husband argued that the assignment provision was meant only to ensure the injured spouse received a liquid asset, so that he should have received offsetting community property to equalize the division. The Court of Appeal rejected that reading and affirmed, holding that the provision directing that community property personal injury damages "shall be assigned to the party who suffered the injuries" was intended to be an exception to the equal division mandate. The court also described what the provision is designed to do: assure that, other than in exceptional circumstances, such damages or the bulk of them will be awarded to the injured spouse, and that under no circumstances will the injured spouse receive less than one-half, while leaving the court discretion in exceptional circumstances to assign the damages in such proportions as it determines to be just.

expectedJSON.body: Both the community-property rule of section 780 and the separate-property rule of section 781 turn on when the cause of action "arose." In Klug v. Klug (2005) 130 Cal.App.4th 1389, the Court of Appeal addressed a postjudgment motion to divide an allegedly omitted community asset — a $346,000 settlement of one spouse’s legal malpractice lawsuit against the couple’s former attorney — and set out the framework of sections 780, 781, and 2603. The court stated that for purposes of a motion to divide an omitted asset, the characterization of tort damages as separate or community property turns on when the cause of action arose. It then distinguished "arose" from "accrued," explaining that a cause of action may arise when the wrongful conduct causes damage even though, under the delayed-discovery rules that govern statutes of limitation, the same cause of action does not accrue until the injured person discovers or should discover the facts. The court concluded that it could think of no policy reason why characterization of a property interest as community or separate should depend on the date of discovery rather than the date all the elements of the cause of action were established, and it affirmed the order treating the settlement as the injured spouse’s separate property.

expectedJSON.body: Not every payment that follows an injury is governed by the personal injury characterization statutes. In In re Marriage of Fisk (1992) 2 Cal.App.4th 1698, a spouse sought a share of, or reimbursement from, a workers’ compensation permanent disability award the other spouse received after the parties separated. The Court of Appeal held that such an award received after separation compensates the injured person for impairment of future earning capacity and is that person’s separate property, and that the reimbursement provision then codified at former Civil Code section 5126, subdivision (b), did not apply. The court reasoned that a workers’ compensation permanent disability award is distinguishable from a personal injury recovery at law — among other reasons, because it is awarded without regard to fault — and that such a disability award therefore cannot be embraced within the term "damages" used in the section’s reimbursement requirement. In a footnote, the court added that the predecessor of section 2603 likewise applies only to personal injury awards in actions at law and had no application to the award.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 782 addresses the source of funds that answers for a liability when an injury to a married person is caused in whole or in part by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of that person’s spouse. Subdivision (a) provides that the community property may not be used to discharge the tortfeasor spouse’s liability to the injured spouse, or the liability to make contribution to a joint tortfeasor, until the separate property of the tortfeasor spouse that is not exempt from enforcement of a money judgment is exhausted. Subdivision (b) states an exception: the section does not prevent the use of community property to discharge such a liability if the injured spouse gives written consent after the occurrence of the injury. Subdivision (c) provides that the section does not affect the right to indemnity provided by an insurance or other contract to discharge the tortfeasor spouse’s liability, whether or not the consideration given for the contract consisted of community property.
